# "I Can't Get Started": The Story Behind a Jazz Standard

The song "I Can't Get Started" holds a distinguished place in American jazz history, largely due to its indelible association with trumpeter Bunny Berigan. Berigan first recorded the tune in 1936, leading a small ensemble that included pianist Joe Bushkin, drummer Cozy Cole, and clarinetist Artie Shaw—a lineup of considerable talent that gave the recording an intimate, chamber-jazz quality distinct from the arrangement that would later make Berigan famous.

Before it became a jazz vehicle, however, "I Can't Get Started" had its origins on the Broadway stage. Written by lyricist Ira Gershwin and composer Vernon Duke, the song debuted in *The Ziegfeld Follies*, where it was originally performed as a duet by Bob Hope and Eve Arden. In this theatrical context, the song functioned as a comic number, its lyrics playing on the incongruity between the singer's worldly accomplishments and his utter failure in matters of the heart.

It was Berigan's 1937 re-recording of the song with a full big band, however, that transformed it into something else entirely—a signature tune inseparable from his name and one of the era's most recognizable trumpet performances. The recording's combination of Berigan's soaring, emotionally direct trumpet playing and his plaintive vocal delivery struck a chord with audiences and fellow musicians alike. So thoroughly did Berigan reshape the song's identity that other prominent artists soon offered their own interpretations. Notably, Billie Holiday recorded a celebrated version not long after, backed by tenor saxophonist Lester Young and members of the Count Basie Orchestra, further cementing the song's status within the jazz canon.

Berigan's relationship with the song was intertwined with his personal life as well. He was romantically involved with singer Lee Wiley, and the two performed together on her CBS radio program, *Saturday Night Swing Club*, beginning in 1936. Despite this close musical and personal partnership, Wiley did not commit "I Can't Get Started" to record until 1945, when she cut an informal version of the ballad—the only time she recorded the song.

Berigan's own story, unfortunately, ended in tragedy. He died in 1942, his health destroyed by complications related to alcoholism, at the age of just thirty-three. Yet the song he made famous carries within its lyrics a trace of the turbulent era in which it was written: a reference to the Spanish Civil War, the conflict that convulsed Spain from 1936 to 1939. This topical allusion, tucked into an otherwise lighthearted lament about romantic failure, serves as a small but telling reminder of the historical moment from which both the song and its most famous interpreter emerged.

# The Legacy of "I Can't Get Started"

"I Can't Get Started" stands as one of the most enduring standards to emerge from the golden age of American popular song, its history intertwined with the tragic career of trumpeter and bandleader Bunny Berigan, who did more than perhaps anyone else to establish the tune as a jazz classic. The song itself was born in 1936, a product of the songwriting partnership between composer Vernon Duke and lyricist Ira Gershwin, and it made its public debut in that year's edition of The Ziegfeld Follies, the storied Broadway revue that had long served as a launching pad for popular songs.

Berigan's association with the composition began almost immediately, and he approached it in two distinct incarnations that would come to define its early reception among jazz audiences. His first recording captured the song in an intimate small-group setting, allowing his virtuosic trumpet playing to weave through the melody with a kind of conversational ease. It was his second treatment, however, recorded in 1937 with his own big band, that transformed the song into something larger than a mere popular tune—it became Berigan's signature piece, the number most closely associated with his name and the one audiences most demanded to hear him play. His extended trumpet solo, with its dramatic high notes and melancholy phrasing, seemed to capture something essential about the song's themes of romantic frustration and unfulfilled longing.

Berigan's personal life, though, was marked by struggles with alcoholism that would ultimately cut short both his career and his life. He died in 1942, still a relatively young man, his talent undiminished but his body ravaged by years of heavy drinking. This premature death meant that Berigan would never live to hear one particular rendition of the song that might have interested him greatly—a performance by singer Lee Wiley, who had been both his romantic partner and professional collaborator during parts of his career.

Wiley's connection to "I Can't Get Started" presents one of the more curious footnotes in the song's history. By all accounts, her vocal style—intimate, slightly husky, emotionally direct—seemed perfectly suited to the song's wistful, self-deprecating lyrics about a man who can seemingly accomplish anything except win the affection of the woman he loves. Musicians and critics who knew her work often remarked that the song might have become one of her signature numbers, much as it had been for Berigan. Yet despite this apparent natural fit, Wiley only performed the song once in any documented capacity, and even that instance was an informal occasion in 1945, three years after Berigan's death, rather than a proper studio recording or concert performance.

This singular, informal rendition meant that Wiley's interpretation of the song never entered the broader public consciousness in the way that other performances did. The song's legacy instead came to be shaped by a constellation of other artists who took up the composition in the years following Berigan's landmark recordings. Chief among these was Billie Holiday, whose celebrated version with the Count Basie Orchestra brought new emotional depths to the material, her distinctive phrasing and sense of timing lending the lyrics an additional layer of poignancy that many listeners found even more affecting than the original Berigan renditions.

The result is a somewhat paradoxical historical narrative: despite Wiley's personal and professional closeness to Berigan, and despite critics' consensus that the song suited her artistic temperament, she remains a minor footnote in its performance history rather than a central figure. # Bunny Berigan: The Trumpet Voice of the Swing Era

Bunny Berigan remains one of the most celebrated trumpet players in American jazz history, a musician whose brilliant career burned brightly but tragically short during the golden age of swing.

Born Rowland Bernart Berigan in 1908 in Hilbert, Wisconsin, he earned the nickname "Bunny" in childhood, a moniker that would follow him throughout his musical career. He developed into one of the most technically gifted and emotionally expressive trumpet players of his generation, distinguished by his warm tone, powerful high register, and remarkable improvisational skills.

Berigan's talents brought him into collaboration with some of the biggest names in jazz and swing music. He performed with the orchestras of Benny Goodman and Tommy Dorsey, contributing memorable solos that helped define the sound of the swing era. His playing on Goodman's "King Porter Stomp" and other recordings showcased his ability to combine technical precision with genuine emotional depth.

However, Berigan is perhaps most remembered for a single, extraordinary recording: "I Can't Get Started." Recorded in 1937 with his own orchestra, this song became his signature piece and one of the most beloved recordings in jazz history. The combination of his soulful trumpet playing and distinctive vocal delivery created a performance of remarkable poignancy. The song's blend of witty lyrics about worldly accomplishment juxtaposed against romantic failure resonated deeply with audiences, and Berigan's interpretation elevated it to legendary status.

Despite his musical success, Berigan struggled throughout his life with alcoholism, which increasingly affected his health and career. Leading his own big band proved financially challenging, and personal difficulties mounted even as his artistic reputation grew. He died in 1942 at just 33 years old, a loss that stunned the jazz community and cut short what many believed would have been an even more remarkable legacy.

Today, Bunny Berigan is remembered as a quintessential figure of the swing era—a musician whose technical brilliance and emotional authenticity captured something essential about American jazz. "I Can't Get Started" continues to be performed and recorded by musicians who recognize it as a masterpiece, ensuring that Berigan's artistic voice, though silenced too soon, continues to resonate with new generations of listeners.
